title: A Second Decree and a Day of Joy
summary: The king gives Haman's estate to Esther and his signet ring to Mordecai, but Haman's decree cannot be revoked. Esther weeps and pleads again, and the king allows Mordecai to write a new edict in the king's name permitting the Jews to assemble and defend themselves on the thirteenth of Adar. Couriers carry it across the empire, Mordecai appears in royal robes, and the Jews celebrate while many of the peoples of the land side with them.
story: Haman is dead at the end of chapter 7, but his edict is still in force, and in the Persian system it cannot simply be canceled. Esther's first plea saved her own life; her second, in this chapter, is for her people. Mordecai, who spent chapter 4 in sackcloth outside the king's gate, now receives Haman's ring, estate, and authority, and walks out of the palace in royal garments. The chapter reverses chapter 3 almost line by line: a new decree, written by new hands, carried by the same system of couriers, answers the old one. Chapter 9 will show what happens when the appointed day arrives.
historical:
The date of the new decree is the twenty-third day of the third month, Sivan (roughly late spring), in about 474 BC, around two months after Haman's edict was issued on the thirteenth of the first month (3:12). That leaves some nine months before the thirteenth of Adar, the twelfth month, when both decrees would take effect. Persian administration used satraps (governors of the great regions), local governors, and princes, and the book's 127 provinces probably refers to smaller administrative districts within the satrapies. The empire's reach from India to Cush (the upper Nile region south of Egypt) matches its extent under Darius I and Xerxes.

The Persian courier system was famous in the ancient world. Herodotus describes relays of horsemen stationed along the royal roads, each riding one stage and passing the message on, so that nothing stopped them. The book's mounted couriers riding horses from the royal stables reflect that network. Documents were written in each people's own script and language, which fits the multilingual administration of the empire; Aramaic served as a common language of government, while inscriptions of Darius were set up in Old Persian, Elamite, and Akkadian.
cultural:
A signet ring was an official's signature. Pressed into clay or wax, its seal made a document the king's own command. Giving the ring to Mordecai put the king's authority in his hands, as Pharaoh did for Joseph (Genesis 41:42). The irrevocability of a Persian royal decree, stated in verse 8 and in Daniel 6:8, meant that the king could not simply withdraw Haman's edict without undermining the authority of his word. The solution was a counter-decree that authorized self-defense.

Mordecai's robes of blue and white, purple garment of fine linen, and large gold crown mark him as a high royal official; blue and white hangings adorned the king's own palace (1:6). The chapter ends with feasting and a surprising note: many of the peoples of the land became Jews, or declared themselves to be on the side of the Jews, because fear of the Jews had fallen on them. Whether this means religious conversion, political alignment, or both is debated.
literary: Much of this chapter deliberately repeats the wording of chapter 3, where Haman's edict was written. The same scribes are called, the same list of officials and provinces appears, the same royal ring seals the letters, and the same couriers ride out. Even the permission to destroy, kill, and annihilate echoes Haman's wording. The effect is a mirror: every instrument once used against the Jews is now used for them. The chapter moves from grief (Esther weeping at the king's feet) to celebration (light, gladness, joy, and honor), and the four nouns in verse 16 pile up to express the flood of relief. The reversal of mourning into joy will become the theme of Purim.

outline.t: Esther and Mordecai receive Haman's estate and ring
The king authorizes a new decree
Mordecai's edict is written and sent
Mordecai in royal robes and the joy of the Jews

doctrines.note: The same channels that carried the threat of death now carry the means of life. The chapter shows God's hidden governance turning the enemy's instruments into tools of deliverance.

The Jews are not rescued by the cancellation of the old decree, which cannot be undone, but by a new word from the king that gives them life on the day of danger. The deliverance is real, public, and celebrated.
Verse 17 records that many from the peoples of the land joined themselves to the Jews. Even in a book that never names God, the rescue of Israel draws outsiders toward his people.

words.note: Chatam, to seal. A sealed document carried the full authority of the one whose seal it bore. Verse 8 states that a decree written in the king's name and sealed with his ring cannot be revoked, which is why the new decree must answer the old one rather than erase it.

Yahad, to become a Jew or to identify as a Jew. The verb occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible. Many of the people of the land became Jews. Scholars debate whether this describes true conversion, a claim of Jewish identity out of fear, or siding with the Jews politically.

Orah, light. The Jews had light and gladness, joy and honor. The word here is a picture of relief and prosperity after darkness, and this verse became part of Jewish ritual: it is recited in the Havdalah blessing at the close of the Sabbath.

Naqam, to avenge. The Jews are permitted to be ready to avenge themselves on their enemies. In the Old Testament vengeance is often rightful vindication or just retribution, not personal spite, and the context here is defense against a decree of annihilation.

christ: The chapter's shape, an irrevocable sentence of death answered not by its cancellation but by a new decree that brings life, has long reminded Christian readers of the gospel. The link is thematic, not predictive: Esther says nothing of a Messiah. But the New Testament does speak of a death sentence that stands against humanity and of a new word from God that gives life, so that “there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Mordecai, dressed in royal robes and trusted with the king's authority, and the outsiders who join the Jews, also foreshadow in a broad way the gospel's picture of a people drawn from every nation into the family of God.

hard.q: Does Mordecai's decree permit the killing of women and children?
hard.a: Verse 8:11 in many translations, including the BSB, reads as though the Jews were allowed to kill the women and children of those who attacked them, echoing the wording of Haman's decree in 3:13. That reading troubles many readers. Some Hebrew scholars argue that the phrase more naturally describes the Jews' own women and children as those whom the enemy forces would attack, so that the decree permits the Jews to defend themselves against anyone who would assault them, their women, and their children. The grammar allows both readings, and translators differ. It is also important that chapter 9, which reports what actually happened, counts men killed in Susa, says nothing of women or children, and stresses that the Jews did not take plunder. Whatever the precise sense of the decree, the book presents it as a defensive answer to a legal order for genocide, not as a license for random slaughter.

questions: Esther pleads again even after her own safety is secure. What would it look like to keep advocating for others after your own crisis has passed?
The old decree could not be revoked, only answered. Are there consequences in your life that can't be undone but can be met with a new word of grace?
Many outsiders joined the Jews when they saw what happened. What draws people toward a community of faith in times of crisis?
